label: Technical / email / serious business communications

corpus: Sent email, Gmail 2015-2026: 677 sent messages measured (643 cleaned openings; 112 sentences from 10 full bodies). Content treated as style-only and never retained.
Academic paper: 'FEA based impedance method for designing active structures' (Littlefield, J.A. Fairweather, Craig; Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute) - full technical prose read.

measurement_status.correspondence: MEASURED - 677 emails over 11 years; the numbers below are counted.
measurement_status.formal_technical: v1 - characterized from one full paper read. Patterns are real (evidence, not inference) but the numeric rates are not yet precisely counted. A count pass and, ideally, the full solo PhD thesis would promote it.

source.privacy: Built from real correspondence and a technical paper. NO sensitive content (clients, dollar figures, legal matters, deals) is stored - only how he writes. Every example is a neutral invention, not a real message.

note: This bucket holds TWO registers James groups under 'business'. They are different - almost opposite on several axes. Choose by medium: correspondence for email/messages, formal_technical for reports/specs/papers.

correspondence.label: Email and business messages
correspondence.one_line: Warm-but-brisk operator voice. Open on the name, do the business in a few short lines - often as questions, not orders - close with thanks, sign JAF.
correspondence.one_line_gestalt: 'Name -' opener, spaced hyphens everywhere, near-zero em-dashes, short punchy sentences with frequent direct questions, numbered lists for anything multi-part, occasional '...' trail-off, one friendly exclamation, signed JAF.

salutation.dominant: 'FirstName -' (name + spaced hyphen): 34% of all openings, ~63% of the ~54% that carry any salutation. The signature greeting ('Mike -', 'Chris -').
salutation.other: ~46% dive straight in, no salutation (quick / mobile replies); Hi/Hello/Hey 16%, often still hyphenated ('Hey Sarah -'); 'FirstName,' with a comma only ~3%. Multiple recipients listed by name, occasionally the rare em-dash ('Priya, Tom -').

sign_off.dominant: 'JAF' (initials), by a wide margin - usually stacked under a short closer: 'Best' / 'Very best' / 'Thanks' + JAF.
sign_off.variants: 'James' (full first name) in warmer or more formal notes and mobile replies; joint 'JAF & DM' / 'James and Day' when writing with Day.
sign_off.note: No standing title/credential block in personal Gmail - sign-offs are short initials or first name, not a formal signature.

punctuation.spaced_hyphen_note: The defining tell - an all-purpose connective dash mid-sentence and after names. The email register's substitute for the essay em-dash, which is effectively zero here.
punctuation.ellipsis_note: A real habit - trailing off at the end of a thought or softening a close ('Would love to help...').

sentences.shape: Bimodal - clipped logistics sentences plus the occasional long reflective one. Short and punchy by default; long only when the topic warrants.
sentences.email_length: Highly variable - quick replies 5-40 words, substantive notes 120-250+.

questions_and_exclamations.questions_note: ~10% of sentences end in '?'. He asks directly and often, and frames asks AS questions ('Would 2:15 work?', 'Can you please send the timeline?') rather than as imperatives.
questions_and_exclamations.exclamations_note: Warm but not gushing - about one per email when present, on a friendly beat.

register_signals.contractions: Moderate and register-signaling: warm/personal emails contract freely ('I'd', 'we'll', 'can't'); serious or firm-tone emails deliberately spell out ('I am', 'do not', 'it does not seem reasonable'). The contraction rate itself marks the register.
register_signals.fragments: Frequent and intentional - standalone short lines: 'All set.', 'Great.', 'Thanks.', 'Best Mark'.

lexicon.abbreviations: Light-touch: FYI (common), LMK, occasional ASAP/Thx. NOT a heavy-acronym writer - no OOO/EOD/COB observed.
lexicon.warm_openers: Present but specific, not formulaic (~8% 'Thanks...', ~4% 'Hope all is well', ~2% 'Great to connect'). Feels particular when it appears.

tells: Numbered lists ('1) ... 2) ... 3)') to structure any multi-topic email - very characteristic.
Name dropped mid-sentence for warmth/emphasis ('Thanks Jon -').
Action-closers: 'Please advise', 'LMK if/when I can be helpful', 'Let me know if there is any follow-up'.
Relational reassurance in business notes ('No agenda; I find the problem genuinely interesting and would enjoy being helpful').
Firmness rises via longer declarative sentences, never caps or extra punctuation.
Occasional capitalized common noun for weight ('Holiday').
examples_neutral: Warm opener: 'Hope the week is treating you well.'
Ask as question: 'Can you please send the updated timeline so we can lock the schedule?'
Numbered: '1) All set on my end. 2) Let me know if the noon slot still works.'
Short direct question: 'Does Thursday afternoon work for a quick call?'
Trailing close: 'Would love to help make this happen...'
Sign-off warm or joint: 'Thanks so much - JAF' / 'James and Day'
never: Corporate throat-clearing ('I am reaching out to', 'per my last email')
Coldness - always at least one warm or courteous beat
Em-dashes (that's the essay voice; email uses the spaced hyphen)

formal_technical.label: Reports, specs, papers, serious technical writing
formal_technical.one_line: Precise, structured, impersonal. Signpost the path, name the mechanism exactly, state the limits honestly. This is the INVERSE of the essay voice - do not apply jaf-longform's rules here.
formal_technical.opening: DO front-load and roadmap (opposite of the essays). An abstract states method and result up front; the intro surveys prior approaches, then: 'First... Then... The experimental results will then be compared to the theory.' The preamble the essays forbid is required here.
formal_technical.structure: Numbered sections with headers, tables, figures, equations - all expected. Build by orderly argument and comparison ('Of the methods mentioned, only the impedance method... comes close to meeting all three requirements'), not by extension.
formal_technical.voice: Passive and third-person for results ('The method is found to accurately predict', 'Comparisons are made'); 'we' for method steps ('we will now show how to get the moment impedances'); never 'I'. NAME the mechanism precisely - eigenvectors, impedance, admittance, boundary conditions - the opposite of the essay's 'inhabit the mechanism, never name it'.
formal_technical.hedging: Hedge honestly and technically - 'may not be a good representation', 'should be extendable', 'comes close to meeting', 'not as good as those for the aluminum plate, but were the best that could be obtained'. Stating a limitation is part of the rigor. (The essays forbid all hedging; here it is mandatory.)
formal_technical.sentences: Moderate and fairly uniform length (not bimodal). Complex, qualified clauses. Nominalizations - 'the determination of the impedances', 'the recovery of the response'.
formal_technical.citations: By numbered reference, not by name-with-honorific.
formal_technical.punctuation: Standard - periods, commas, colons. Few or no em-dashes. Semicolons acceptable here (unlike every other register).

contrast_with_longform: Same author, opposite instincts by register. Essays: back-load, no preamble, no hedge, inhabit-never-name, no headers, em-dash breath unit. Technical: front-load, signpost, hedge honestly, name precisely, full apparatus, standard punctuation. Email sits between: warm and brief like the essays, but transactional, spaced-hyphened, question-driven, and numbered - not lyrical. Never draft a report in the essay voice or an essay in the report voice.
